paragraphs.text: An oolong from [Nantou](nantou:where-it-is), the county in the middle of Taiwan and the only one that does not touch the sea. Nantou is the island's [biggest tea county](nantou:why-people-value-it). Its land climbs from low hills to cold mountain gardens, and where in the county a tea grew decides whether it is made in the [roasted way or the high mountain way](nantou:altitude-bands). This record names only the county, not the township or mountain.

It is rolled [oolong](oolong:definition), the partly oxidised tea that sits between green and red tea. It belongs to the [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) line, whose plants and craft came over from Fujian.

Made in 1979, it has now been kept for forty-seven years. Taiwan has its own tradition of keeping oolong, called [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), or old tea. The leaf chosen for keeping starts dry and well roasted. It is roasted again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in, and it is stored cool, dark and sealed. No standard says when an oolong becomes old. Those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty years, and this tea is well past the longest of them.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
